arguments.text: Evidence batch: Rewards for Justice describes Conti, also known as Wizard Spider, as a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service group targeting US and Western critical infrastructure. It says aliases Target, Reshaev, Professor, Tramp, and Dandis are believed linked to Conti; associated location Russia; associated applications include Conti ransomware-as-a-service, TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader. It reports first detection in 2019, more than 1,000 operations, over 400 organizations worldwide victimized and over 290 in the US, with theft and encryption, ransom portals, and publication/sale of stolen data if unpaid; demands up to $25m. It says operators pledged support to Russia after February 2022 invasion and threatened infrastructure of countries perceived hostile to Russia. Rapid7 reports @ContiLeaks released 14MB of chats in 393 JSON files on Feb 27, 2022; some encrypted, so incomplete. Leaks included internal communications, tools, exploits/design processes, credentials, alleged server access, and alleged source code; Rapid7 says the leaker was likely a senior member or coalition of disgruntled affiliates. Rapid7 describes hiring/interviews, coding exercises, salary negotiations, product development, Bitcoin holdings, alleged FSB funding discussion, coders, testers, phishing, control panel, operators, third-party malicious documents, and ongoing operations after infrastructure takedown. CIS reports Conti as a notorious RaaS using double extortion and possible ties to TrickBot; leaks described business units and specialized roles: Coders, Testers, Administrators, Reverse Engineers, Penetration Testers/Hackers, with spamming contracted out; more than 60 employees claimed by an insider in July 2021. CIS says Conti platform shut down/rebranded into smaller units in May 2022 and leak/negotiation infrastructure shut down about a month later. CIS explains RaaS as developers leasing malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share profits, often 70/30, and initial access brokers selling access. DOJ Middle District of Tennessee page lists cases 3:23-CR-00092 against Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, and 3:23-CR-00088 against Oleksii Lytvynenko. DOJ says Conti affected more than 900 victims worldwide; the four 2023 defendants are charged with CFAA and wire-fraud conspiracies, and Lytvynenko is charged with conspiracy to deploy Conti. DOJ explicitly says defendants are presumed innocent. As of June 10, 2026 DOJ page says Lytvynenko pleaded guilty to Count 2 conspiracy to commit wire fraud, with sentencing scheduled Sept 10, 2026.

# CASE BACKGROUND

This investigation concerns the public record regarding Conti ransomware, the ContiLeaks disclosures, alleged Russian links, associated malware and infrastructure, and U.S. criminal proceedings involving alleged Conti-related actors.

The supplied evidence consists only of benchmark sources [SRC-001]–[SRC-004]. No source URLs were included in the case context; therefore, no URLs have been invented. Citations below preserve the supplied source identifiers.

# GENERAL OBJECTIVES

1. Establish Conti’s publicly reported aliases, affiliations, and operational profile.
2. Assess what the ContiLeaks archive publicly disclosed and its evidentiary limitations.
3. Document Conti’s ransomware business model, malware ecosystem, and operational structure.
4. Summarize the U.S. criminal cases and distinguish charges from adjudicated findings.
5. Identify attribution uncertainties, allegations, and apparent inconsistencies in the public record.

# LEGAL ISSUES

- [SRC-001] characterizes Conti as a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service group. This is a public attribution statement, not a judicial finding.
- [SRC-002] reports an alleged conversation concerning Russian Federal Security Service involvement in some funding and interest in Bellingcat and Navalny-related files. Rapid7 presents this as an allegation or assessment, not an adjudicated fact.
- [SRC-004] reports charges against named defendants for alleged CFAA, wire-fraud, and Conti-deployment conspiracies. The defendants are presumed innocent.
- [SRC-004] reports that Oleksii Lytvynenko pleaded guilty on 2026-06-10 to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, with sentencing scheduled for 2026-09-10.
- No supplied source establishes that any named defendant was one of the aliases Target, Reshaev, Professor, Tramp, or Dandis, nor that any such alias is a legal identity.

# INVESTIGATION PREPARATION

The assessment was limited to the four supplied benchmark sources:

- [SRC-001] Rewards for Justice material concerning Conti’s aliases, Russian association, victims, methods, and threats.
- [SRC-002] Rapid7 analysis of the ContiLeaks archive and Conti’s internal operations.
- [SRC-003] Center for Internet Security analysis of Conti’s RaaS model, organizational structure, and later shutdown/rebranding.
- [SRC-004] U.S. Department of Justice, Middle District of Tennessee, criminal-case information.

The analysis distinguishes between:

- reported facts and source characterizations;
- allegations and assessments;
- criminal charges and convictions or guilty pleas;
- operational metrics that measure different things.

# OSINT STEPS

1. Compared the aliases and affiliations reported in [SRC-001] with the supplied knowledge-base relations.
2. Reviewed the scope and limitations of the ContiLeaks archive described in [SRC-002].
3. Compared Conti’s operational structure and malware ecosystem across [SRC-001], [SRC-002], and [SRC-003].
4. Compared the victim and operation figures reported by [SRC-001] and [SRC-004].
5. Reviewed the criminal matters and procedural status reported by [SRC-004].
6. Tested whether any supplied source connects the five public aliases to a named defendant; none does.
7. Recorded unresolved contradictions and limitations without treating them as proof of fabrication or concealment.

# FINDINGS

## 1. Identity, aliases, and attribution

[SRC-001] states that Conti is also known as Wizard Spider and describes it as a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service group targeting U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. The same source says the aliases Target, Reshaev, Professor, Tramp, and Dandis are believed to be linked to Conti and associates Conti with Russia.

The available record supports reporting these as public aliases or suspected aliases, not verified legal identities. No supplied source links any of those aliases to Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, or Oleksii Lytvynenko. [SRC-001] [SRC-004]

## 2. ContiLeaks disclosures and limitations

[SRC-002] reports that @ContiLeaks released approximately 14 MB of chat logs in 393 JSON files on 2022-02-27. The archive included internal communications, discussions of tools and exploits, credentials, alleged server access, and alleged source code. Some files were encrypted, making the archive incomplete.

Rapid7 assessed that the leaker was likely a senior member or a coalition of disgruntled affiliates. The chats reportedly showed recruitment, interviews, coding exercises, salary negotiations, product development, coders and operators, testing, phishing, control-panel development, and use of third-party malicious documents. These are source assessments; the supplied material does not establish that every allegation in the chats was authentic, complete, or independently verified. [SRC-002]

## 3. Business model, malware ecosystem, and scale

Conti is described as a double-extortion ransomware-as-a-service operation. Under the RaaS model, developers lease or provide malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share proceeds, often under a 70/30 arrangement; initial-access brokers may separately sell access. [SRC-003]

The reported ecosystem includes Conti ransomware-as-a-service, TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader. [SRC-001] Conti also reportedly maintained specialized roles including coders, testers, administrators, reverse engineers, and penetration testers or hackers. Spamming was reportedly contracted externally, and the organization allegedly maintained separate budgets and borrowing arrangements. An insider cited by [SRC-003] claimed that Conti had more than 60 employees in July 2021.

[SRC-001] reports more than 1,000 ransomware operations and more than 400 victim organizations worldwide, including over 290 in the United States. [SRC-004] separately reports that Conti affected more than 900 victims worldwide. These figures use different metrics and may reflect different counting methods or time periods; neither source alone resolves the difference.

## 4. ContiLeaks and alleged Russian security-service connections

[SRC-002] reports a conversation allegedly indicating Russian FSB involvement in some funding and interest in Bellingcat and Navalny-related files. This should be treated as an allegation reported by Rapid7, not as an adjudicated or independently established fact.

[SRC-001] separately describes Conti as Russian government-linked and reports that, after Russia’s February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Conti pledged support for Russia and threatened infrastructure in countries perceived to be at war with Russia. The supplied evidence therefore documents a significant public attribution record, but it does not establish the precise nature, command structure, or legal proof of any state relationship. [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

## 5. Infrastructure shutdown, rebranding, and continued activity

[SRC-002] reports that Conti took down exposed infrastructure and had resumed normal operations by 2022-03-09. [SRC-003] reports that the Conti platform shut down or rebranded into smaller units in May 2022, with leak and negotiation infrastructure shut down approximately one month later.

These accounts are not necessarily mutually exclusive: they may concern different infrastructure, operational layers, or dates. The sources support a conclusion that Conti experienced exposure-related disruption and later organizational or platform changes, but they do not establish a single precise shutdown event. [SRC-002] [SRC-003]

## 6. U.S. criminal cases

[SRC-004] identifies case 3:23-CR-00092 involving Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, and Andrey Zhuykov. The defendants were charged with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

The same source identifies case 3:23-CR-00088 involving Oleksii Lytvynenko, charged with conspiracy to deploy Conti. [SRC-004] also reports that Lytvynenko pleaded guilty on 2026-06-10 to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, with sentencing scheduled for 2026-09-10.

The charges and reported plea establish procedural events, not proof that the defendants used any of the five aliases or that they constituted the entire Conti organization. Defendants other than the reported guilty-plea subject remain presumed innocent under the supplied record. [SRC-004]

# CONCLUSION

The supplied sources portray Conti as a large, Russian-associated ransomware-as-a-service ecosystem with a double-extortion model, specialized internal roles, affiliate participation, and links to a broader malware ecosystem including TrickBot. [SRC-001] [SRC-003]

The ContiLeaks archive provides unusually detailed insight into the group’s internal organization, recruitment, technical work, finances, and alleged relationships. However, the archive was incomplete because some files were encrypted, and several high-impact claims—particularly alleged FSB funding or involvement—remain allegations or source assessments rather than adjudicated findings. [SRC-002]

The public attribution record supports associating Conti with Wizard Spider, Russia, and the aliases Target, Reshaev, Professor, Tramp, and Dandis as suspected aliases. It does not establish that those aliases were the legal identities of any defendant named in [SRC-004]. The reported operation and victim totals are not directly contradictory because they appear to measure different concepts. Likewise, resumed activity in March 2022 and later platform shutdown or rebranding in May 2022 can describe different operational layers or stages.

output.report:
# CASE BACKGROUND

This investigation concerns the public record regarding Conti ransomware, the ContiLeaks disclosures, alleged Russian links, associated malware and infrastructure, and U.S. criminal proceedings involving alleged Conti-related actors.

The supplied evidence consists only of benchmark sources [SRC-001]–[SRC-004]. No source URLs were included in the case context; therefore, no URLs have been invented. Citations below preserve the supplied source identifiers.

# GENERAL OBJECTIVES

1. Establish Conti’s publicly reported aliases, affiliations, and operational profile.
2. Assess what the ContiLeaks archive publicly disclosed and its evidentiary limitations.
3. Document Conti’s ransomware business model, malware ecosystem, and operational structure.
4. Summarize the U.S. criminal cases and distinguish charges from adjudicated findings.
5. Identify attribution uncertainties, allegations, and apparent inconsistencies in the public record.

# LEGAL ISSUES

- [SRC-001] characterizes Conti as a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service group. This is a public attribution statement, not a judicial finding.
- [SRC-002] reports an alleged conversation concerning Russian Federal Security Service involvement in some funding and interest in Bellingcat and Navalny-related files. Rapid7 presents this as an allegation or assessment, not an adjudicated fact.
- [SRC-004] reports charges against named defendants for alleged CFAA, wire-fraud, and Conti-deployment conspiracies. The defendants are presumed innocent.
- [SRC-004] reports that Oleksii Lytvynenko pleaded guilty on 2026-06-10 to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, with sentencing scheduled for 2026-09-10.
- No supplied source establishes that any named defendant was one of the aliases Target, Reshaev, Professor, Tramp, or Dandis, nor that any such alias is a legal identity.

# INVESTIGATION PREPARATION

The assessment was limited to the four supplied benchmark sources:

- [SRC-001] Rewards for Justice material concerning Conti’s aliases, Russian association, victims, methods, and threats.
- [SRC-002] Rapid7 analysis of the ContiLeaks archive and Conti’s internal operations.
- [SRC-003] Center for Internet Security analysis of Conti’s RaaS model, organizational structure, and later shutdown/rebranding.
- [SRC-004] U.S. Department of Justice, Middle District of Tennessee, criminal-case information.

The analysis distinguishes between:

- reported facts and source characterizations;
- allegations and assessments;
- criminal charges and convictions or guilty pleas;
- operational metrics that measure different things.

# OSINT STEPS

1. Compared the aliases and affiliations reported in [SRC-001] with the supplied knowledge-base relations.
2. Reviewed the scope and limitations of the ContiLeaks archive described in [SRC-002].
3. Compared Conti’s operational structure and malware ecosystem across [SRC-001], [SRC-002], and [SRC-003].
4. Compared the victim and operation figures reported by [SRC-001] and [SRC-004].
5. Reviewed the criminal matters and procedural status reported by [SRC-004].
6. Tested whether any supplied source connects the five public aliases to a named defendant; none does.
7. Recorded unresolved contradictions and limitations without treating them as proof of fabrication or concealment.

# FINDINGS

## 1. Identity, aliases, and attribution

[SRC-001] states that Conti is also known as Wizard Spider and describes it as a Russian government-linked ransomware-as-a-service group targeting U.S. and Western critical infrastructure. The same source says the aliases Target, Reshaev, Professor, Tramp, and Dandis are believed to be linked to Conti and associates Conti with Russia.

The available record supports reporting these as public aliases or suspected aliases, not verified legal identities. No supplied source links any of those aliases to Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, Andrey Zhuykov, or Oleksii Lytvynenko. [SRC-001] [SRC-004]

## 2. ContiLeaks disclosures and limitations

[SRC-002] reports that @ContiLeaks released approximately 14 MB of chat logs in 393 JSON files on 2022-02-27. The archive included internal communications, discussions of tools and exploits, credentials, alleged server access, and alleged source code. Some files were encrypted, making the archive incomplete.

Rapid7 assessed that the leaker was likely a senior member or a coalition of disgruntled affiliates. The chats reportedly showed recruitment, interviews, coding exercises, salary negotiations, product development, coders and operators, testing, phishing, control-panel development, and use of third-party malicious documents. These are source assessments; the supplied material does not establish that every allegation in the chats was authentic, complete, or independently verified. [SRC-002]

## 3. Business model, malware ecosystem, and scale

Conti is described as a double-extortion ransomware-as-a-service operation. Under the RaaS model, developers lease or provide malware to affiliates who conduct intrusions and share proceeds, often under a 70/30 arrangement; initial-access brokers may separately sell access. [SRC-003]

The reported ecosystem includes Conti ransomware-as-a-service, TrickBot, IcedID, Cobalt Strike, and ZLoader. [SRC-001] Conti also reportedly maintained specialized roles including coders, testers, administrators, reverse engineers, and penetration testers or hackers. Spamming was reportedly contracted externally, and the organization allegedly maintained separate budgets and borrowing arrangements. An insider cited by [SRC-003] claimed that Conti had more than 60 employees in July 2021.

[SRC-001] reports more than 1,000 ransomware operations and more than 400 victim organizations worldwide, including over 290 in the United States. [SRC-004] separately reports that Conti affected more than 900 victims worldwide. These figures use different metrics and may reflect different counting methods or time periods; neither source alone resolves the difference.

## 4. ContiLeaks and alleged Russian security-service connections

[SRC-002] reports a conversation allegedly indicating Russian FSB involvement in some funding and interest in Bellingcat and Navalny-related files. This should be treated as an allegation reported by Rapid7, not as an adjudicated or independently established fact.

[SRC-001] separately describes Conti as Russian government-linked and reports that, after Russia’s February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, Conti pledged support for Russia and threatened infrastructure in countries perceived to be at war with Russia. The supplied evidence therefore documents a significant public attribution record, but it does not establish the precise nature, command structure, or legal proof of any state relationship. [SRC-001] [SRC-002]

## 5. Infrastructure shutdown, rebranding, and continued activity

[SRC-002] reports that Conti took down exposed infrastructure and had resumed normal operations by 2022-03-09. [SRC-003] reports that the Conti platform shut down or rebranded into smaller units in May 2022, with leak and negotiation infrastructure shut down approximately one month later.

These accounts are not necessarily mutually exclusive: they may concern different infrastructure, operational layers, or dates. The sources support a conclusion that Conti experienced exposure-related disruption and later organizational or platform changes, but they do not establish a single precise shutdown event. [SRC-002] [SRC-003]

## 6. U.S. criminal cases

[SRC-004] identifies case 3:23-CR-00092 involving Maksim Galochkin, Maksim Rudenskiy, Mikhail Tsarev, and Andrey Zhuykov. The defendants were charged with conspiracy to violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

The same source identifies case 3:23-CR-00088 involving Oleksii Lytvynenko, charged with conspiracy to deploy Conti. [SRC-004] also reports that Lytvynenko pleaded guilty on 2026-06-10 to Count 2, conspiracy to commit wire fraud, with sentencing scheduled for 2026-09-10.

The charges and reported plea establish procedural events, not proof that the defendants used any of the five aliases or that they constituted the entire Conti organization. Defendants other than the reported guilty-plea subject remain presumed innocent under the supplied record. [SRC-004]

# CONCLUSION

The supplied sources portray Conti as a large, Russian-associated ransomware-as-a-service ecosystem with a double-extortion model, specialized internal roles, affiliate participation, and links to a broader malware ecosystem including TrickBot. [SRC-001] [SRC-003]

The ContiLeaks archive provides unusually detailed insight into the group’s internal organization, recruitment, technical work, finances, and alleged relationships. However, the archive was incomplete because some files were encrypted, and several high-impact claims—particularly alleged FSB funding or involvement—remain allegations or source assessments rather than adjudicated findings. [SRC-002]

The public attribution record supports associating Conti with Wizard Spider, Russia, and the aliases Target, Reshaev, Professor, Tramp, and Dandis as suspected aliases. It does not establish that those aliases were the legal identities of any defendant named in [SRC-004]. The reported operation and victim totals are not directly contradictory because they appear to measure different concepts. Likewise, resumed activity in March 2022 and later platform shutdown or rebranding in May 2022 can describe different operational layers or stages.

- [SRC-002] Rapid7 source supplied in the case context. Source URL was not included in the supplied materials.
- [SRC-003] Center for Internet Security source supplied in the case context. Source URL was not included in the supplied materials.
